questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The absence of a figure on the Book of Kells Chi Rho page
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a page can carry its subject without a depicted body
questions.stem: Revising the Book of Kells, your study group notes that the Chi Rho page carries the letters of the monogram but no body of Christ. Which reading of that absence best fits the page?

options.text: The letters themselves take the place of the body, so the monogram is the figure and not a frame for one
The figure was painted in a lost layer and nothing survives of it, so the page was left half finished
options.misconception: reads an absent figure as a lost or unfinished passage

options.text: Christ was left out because the letter forms were considered too sacred to share a page with a figure
options.misconception: invents a rule of sanctity to explain an absent figure

options.text: The page was produced in a scriptorium without figure painters, so only the letters were attempted
options.misconception: explains the absence of a figure by the skills available

questions.explanation: In the Kells Chi Rho the monogram is the body: the letters are drawn with the elaboration a figure would receive and carry the meaning without one. Nothing suggests a lost layer or a rule of sanctity.
questions.hint: Ask what the page uses in place of a body.

questions.stem: Your study group, revising the Lindisfarne Gospels, counts the creatures drawn into the letters of the incipit initial: 9 birds, 6 fish and 4 quadrupeds. How many creatures are drawn into the letters altogether?

options.text: Nineteen creatures, because 9 birds plus 6 fish plus 4 quadrupeds gives 19
Eleven creatures, because 9 birds plus 6 fish is counted and the quadrupeds are left out
options.misconception: leaves out one of the three groups of creatures

options.text: Two hundred and sixteen, because 9 birds multiplied by 6 fish multiplied by 4 quadrupeds
options.misconception: multiplies the three counts instead of adding them

options.text: Six creatures, because only the fish are counted as belonging to the letters
options.misconception: counts only one group of creatures as part of the letters

questions.explanation: The three groups are all part of the initial, so 9 plus 6 plus 4 gives 19 creatures. Leaving one group out, multiplying the counts, or counting only one kind each answer a different question.
questions.hint: Add every group the initial contains.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The uncoloured drawing of the Utrecht Psalter
questions.learningObjective: Explain what an uncoloured drawing achieves in a manuscript
questions.stem: During a revision of the Utrecht Psalter, your group asks why a manuscript of drawings kept almost entirely without colour can still be read as a serious work of art. Explain what the uncoloured drawing achieves.

answer.exemplar: The uncoloured drawing in the Utrecht Psalter makes the line do the work that colour would otherwise do, so that the ink, with its light corrections and searching pen strokes, can be read as the thinking hand of the artist rather than a preparatory stage. The drawings are not studies for something else, since each one stands beside the psalm verse it illustrates, and the restraint of the line is what makes the drawn idea legible.

questions.explanation: The uncoloured drawing lets the line carry the whole meaning, so the searching strokes read as the artist's thinking hand rather than a rough stage beside its verse.
questions.hint: Ask what the pen strokes do that colour would otherwise do.

questions.topic: The Coronation Gospels as a pledge object
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a pledge inscription and the image that accompanies it

stimulus.body: A member of the study group brings a note on the Coronation Gospels to the revision session. The note records that the manuscript is inscribed as a gift from the person to whom it was given, that it is described as a pledge, and that it carries an image of an enthroned ruler with a female figure beside him personifying a city. The group is preparing to answer a question about what the manuscript was for.

questions.stem: Your revision group discusses the Coronation Gospels, which is inscribed as a gift and described as a pledge. Which reading of that description best fits the object?

options.text: A book copied for private reading, and the image shows the owner in a devotional pose
options.misconception: reads an enthroned ruler as a private devotional reader

options.text: A gift made to bind a recipient to a giver, with the image showing a ruler in the city he claims
A legal contract, and the image shows a witness signing the terms of the pledge
options.misconception: treats the pledge as a written contract rather than a gift

options.text: A record of a coronation, and the image shows the ruler being crowned at the moment of the gift
options.misconception: turns an inscription about a gift into a coronation record

questions.explanation: The pledge language makes the book a presentation that creates an obligation, and the enthroned ruler with a personified city ties the donor to claims of authority.
questions.hint: Ask what a pledge does that a plain gift does not.

options.misconception: assumes the attendants are later additions to the portrait

options.text: Because medieval artists always enlarged the most important figure without any symbolic intent at all
options.misconception: treats hierarchy of scale as a habit with no meaning

options.text: Because the emperor was physically larger than the delegates who brought the lands to him
options.misconception: reads an image of rule as a record of physical size

Eighteen bands, because the four counts are added and never divided by the number of images

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The absence of a figure on the Book of Kells Chi Rho page
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a missing figure on a page need not be a gap
questions.stem: In your session on the Book of Kells, the group is asked why the absence of a human figure on the Chi Rho page is not simply a gap. Explain what the page does instead of showing a body.

answer.exemplar: On the Chi Rho page the monogram is the body: the chi and rho are drawn with the elaboration that a figure would receive, and the letters are filled with the same combination of ornament, animal forms and interlace that elsewhere carries the imagery. The reader is therefore given Christ as letters rather than as a body, and the page's refusal of a figure is a deliberate choice of medium rather than a failure to finish the work.

questions.explanation: The monogram is drawn with the elaboration a figure would receive, so Christ is given as letters. The missing body is a choice of medium, not an unfinished passage.
questions.hint: Ask what the letters are asked to do in place of a body.

options.text: A set of coloured illuminations with the paint worn away, leaving only the underdrawing
options.misconception: reads an unfinished colour as paint that was once applied

options.text: A cycle of pen drawings in which the line alone carries the image, set beside the verses it illustrates
A book of preparatory sketches made for an illuminator who never completed the work
options.misconception: treats finished drawings as abandoned preparatory studies

options.text: A musical manuscript in which the drawings record the words that were sung
options.misconception: mistakes psalm verses for a sung text

questions.explanation: Each drawing is a finished work set beside its verse, and the line does the work colour would do, so the uncoloured state is the manuscript's character, not a loss.
questions.hint: Ask whether the drawings are finished and what they sit beside.

options.text: Show the ink is iron gall, then treat the fading of the ink as the reason for the broken line
options.misconception: attributes the broken line to the behaviour of the ink

options.text: Show the page is small, then treat the cramped writing as the cause of the nervous line
options.misconception: explains the line by the size of the page rather than the hand

options.text: Show the line breaks from the model's contour, then show the change is carried into the scene
Show the manuscript was made quickly, then treat the agitation as a record of haste
options.misconception: reads a working manner as evidence of speed

questions.explanation: The agitation is a working manner, and it is an expression only if the line is shown to break from the contour and spread into the rest of the picture. Size, ink and haste describe something else.
questions.hint: Ask where the line stops following the form.

questions.stem: On the Coronation Gospels, the group considers why the manuscript records a pledge rather than a simple gift. Which argument best explains the difference?

options.text: A pledge was used for every medieval book, because no other kind of presentation was possible

options.misconception: reads a pledge as a temporary loan returned later

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The enthroned emperor in the Gospels of Otto III
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the personification of lands allows an imperial image to claim
questions.stem: In the Gospels of Otto III, the group is asked why the personified lands are shown as women beside the enthroned emperor. Explain what that convention lets the image claim.

answer.exemplar: By showing the lands as women, the image makes the claim personal and bodily: the emperor holds a court of personified territories who present themselves to him, acknowledge his supremacy and offer the gifts of their provinces. The women are not portraits of queens, and the image is not a marriage scene, but the convention lets the claim of rule over lands be made in a form the viewer can read at once.

questions.explanation: Showing the lands as women makes the claim personal and bodily, a court of territories presenting themselves to the emperor. They are not portraits of queens, and this is not a marriage scene.
questions.hint: Ask what the figures are actually made to stand for.

stimulus.body: A study group member brings a rubbing of the Chi Rho page from the Book of Kells to the revision session. The group is preparing an answer about how the page presents its subject.

questions.stem: A rubbing of the Kells Chi Rho page shows letters packed with interlace, spirals and small creatures, and no body. Which presentation does the page make?

options.text: Christ is shown in a damaged state, since the body was rubbed away over the centuries
options.misconception: reads a missing figure as damage to the surface

options.text: Christ is given as the letters themselves, elaborated in place of a depicted body
Christ is deliberately deferred, since the subject of the page is the text of the Gospel
options.misconception: explains the absent figure by the subject matter of the page

options.text: Christ appears in the initial letter only, so the monogram is a signature rather than a scene
options.misconception: misreads the monogram as a mark of ownership

questions.explanation: The letters are elaborated as a body would be, so the monogram carries the figure itself. The absent body is a choice of medium, not damage, a deferral or a signature.
questions.hint: Ask what the page uses instead of a body.

questions.explanation: A letter is inhabited when figures and animals are drawn into its strokes and the strokes become their bodies. Colour, surrounding ornament and repetition settle something else each.

questions.topic: The Coronation Gospels as a pledge object
questions.learningObjective: Explain what pairing a ruler with a personified city asserts
questions.stem: On the pledge in the Coronation Gospels, the group is asked why the enthroned figure in the manuscript is placed beside a personification of a city. Explain what that pairing lets the image assert.

answer.exemplar: The enthroned ruler is set beside a personified city so that the claim of rule is made twice over: the throne gives him the pose of an emperor, and the city, which is the older and the more universal of the two, offers the recognition of his rule. The pairing is not a portrait of a man with a woman, and it does not record a meeting that happened, but it turns a statement about authority into a statement about a city that submits.

questions.explanation: The throne and the personified city make the claim of rule twice, and the city submits to him. The pairing is not a portrait of a couple and does not record a meeting.
questions.hint: Ask what the city is doing in the image.

answer.exemplar: The monogram is set at a scale no other element on the page approaches, and the ornament of interlace, spirals and creatures is organised to point inward toward the strokes of the two letters. questions.topic: The Coronation Gospels as a pledge object

answer.exemplar: The page does the work of a legal act by naming the giver, the recipient, the object given and the binding pledge, with a prayer for the giver's memory fixed alongside, and it does the work of devotion by making the gift an offering in the presence of the divine. questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The uncoloured drawing of the Utrecht Psalter
questions.learningObjective: Explain what an unframed arrangement does for a book of drawings
questions.stem: On the arrangement of the Utrecht Psalter drawings, the group is asked why they are not set to decorate the pages of the book. Explain what the arrangement does instead.

answer.exemplar: The drawings are placed beside the psalm verses they illustrate rather than in frames or margins, so that each image reads as an argument about the words next to it, and the book can be read as a sequence of statements rather than as a display. The arrangement also leaves the page open, which suits a pen drawing that carries no fill, and it means the reader meets image and text at once instead of finding one set decorating the other.

questions.explanation: Placing each drawing beside its verse makes it an argument about the words rather than decoration of the page. The open arrangement suits drawings that carry no fill.
questions.hint: Ask what the drawing does for the verse beside it.

questions.topic: The agitated line of the Ebbo Gospels evangelist portrait

questions.stem: Counting the broken strokes in the Ebbo Gospels portrait, the group finds 45 in the evangelist's seat and 25 in the drapery of the adjoining figure. How many strokes in total are recorded for the two areas?
questions.explanation: Forty-five strokes in the seat plus 25 in the drapery gives 70 broken strokes in the two areas. The same searching manner governs furniture and drapery as well as flesh.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The Coronation Gospels as a pledge object
questions.learningObjective: Classify a lavish manuscript by the kind of object it is

stimulus.body: A member of the revision group notes that the Coronation Gospels is bound in a treasure binding of gold, gems and pearls over a purple cover, and that the pages themselves are written in gold and silver on purple-dyed parchment, with a painted and gilded dedication page showing an enthroned ruler and a personification of a city. The group is preparing an answer about what kind of object this is.

questions.stem: Your group describes the Coronation Gospels as gold letters on purple parchment in a jeweled binding. What kind of object is it best called?

options.text: A fragment of an earlier book, reused because the older manuscript had been broken up
options.misconception: invents a dismembered predecessor to explain the object

options.text: A working copy, kept for daily reading in the chapter house of a monastery
options.misconception: treats a luxury book as a practical working copy

options.text: A treasure book, made to be seen and handled as a gift that displays the giver's means
A relic, kept because a piece of the true cross was bound into the cover
options.misconception: assumes a jeweled binding must contain a relic

questions.explanation: Gold letters, purple parchment and a jeweled binding make this a treasure book, meant to be seen and handled as a gift. A working copy, a reused fragment and a relic describe something else.
questions.hint: Ask what the object was made to be used for.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The painted and gilded surface of the Gero Crucifix
questions.learningObjective: Set out the conditions for describing a double reading of an object
questions.stem: On the Gero Crucifix, the group asks how the object is read by worshippers and by scholars at the same time. Which two steps does the group need before that double reading can be described?

options.text: Ask how much the carving cost, then treat the cost as a measure of how the figure was received
options.misconception: measures reception by the cost of the commission

options.text: Count the scenes painted on the figure, then treat the number as the measure of its renown
options.misconception: measures renown by the number of painted scenes

options.text: Note the date of the commission, then treat the date as a complete explanation of the object
options.misconception: explains the object by its date alone

options.text: Set out the devotional use of the image, then set out the historical claims the evidence supports

questions.explanation: A double reading needs the devotional use of the image and, separately, the historical claims the evidence supports, kept apart rather than blended. Counting scenes and the commission date measure something else.
questions.hint: Ask what two audiences need before a reading can be given to each.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The enthroned emperor in the Gospels of Otto III
questions.learningObjective: Explain why imperial images belong in a book of Christian text
questions.stem: On the imperial images in the Gospels of Otto III, the group asks how they sit within a book of Christian text. Which argument best explains their presence?

options.text: Because medieval books were illustrated at random, with no relation between image and text
options.misconception: treats illustration as arbitrary in medieval books

options.text: Because the imagery presents the emperor as the setting in which the gospel is heard, and so claims order
Because the emperor paid for the book and so could put his likeness wherever he liked
options.misconception: explains placement by the patron's right to do as he pleased

options.text: Because the illuminators were copying an earlier book and could not alter the design
options.misconception: explains a design as an unalterable copy

questions.explanation: The imperial images claim that the emperor is the order in which the gospel is heard, and they belong in the book for that reason. Random illustration and an unalterable copy are weaker explanations.
questions.hint: Ask what the emperor is made to be in relation to the text.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The flattened ground of the Bamberg Apocalypse
questions.learningObjective: Find the leaves not accounted for by two marked groups
questions.stem: Counting the leaves of the Bamberg Apocalypse, a member records 104 in the original, 8 of them lost, and notes that 11 surviving leaves carry the Genesis images while 82 carry other imagery. How many surviving leaves are not accounted for by those two groups?

options.text: One hundred and eighty-five, because 11 Genesis leaves and 82 other leaves are added together
options.misconception: adds the two groups instead of subtracting them

options.text: Ninety-three leaves, because 11 Genesis leaves are subtracted from the 104 in the original
options.misconception: subtracts from the original total instead of the surviving one

options.text: Three leaves, because 96 surviving leaves less 11 Genesis less 82 other leaves gives 3
Eleven leaves, because the Genesis group is the only one counted within the lost total
options.misconception: counts a group inside the leaves that were lost

questions.explanation: There are 96 surviving leaves, and the two groups account for 93 of them, so 3 are left over. Subtracting from the original total or adding the two groups answers a different question.
questions.hint: Work from the surviving total, then subtract both groups.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The absence of a figure on the Book of Kells Chi Rho page
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a page asks of the person looking at it
questions.stem: In the reading of the Book of Kells, the group is asked what the experience of the Chi Rho page demands of a reader. Explain what the page asks of the person looking at it.

answer.exemplar: The page asks for sustained, close attention rather than a single glance, because the interlace and the animal forms are resolved only as the eye moves over them, and the letters themselves can be read as figures only after that work of looking. The result is a page in which the subject is present as a difficulty to be resolved rather than as an image to be recognised at once, which is a very different experience from reading a picture of the same subject.

questions.explanation: The page asks for sustained attention, because the ornament resolves only as the eye moves and the letters read as figures only after that work of looking. The subject is a difficulty to be resolved.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader has to do to read this page.

questions.topic: The inhabited initial of the Lindisfarne Gospels incipit
questions.learningObjective: Add two selected groups of letters from an initial
questions.stem: Counting the Lindisfarne Gospels incipit letters, the group finds 9 in the initial, of which 4 are formed from interlace and 3 from animal bodies. How many letters are formed from interlace or animal bodies?
questions.explanation: Four letters formed from interlace plus 3 formed from animal bodies gives 7 of the 9 letters. The remaining 2 are formed in a single stroke without either treatment.
questions.hint: Add the two named groups of letters together.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The uncoloured drawing of the Utrecht Psalter
questions.learningObjective: Describe the making of drawings that keep their corrections visible

stimulus.body: A member of the study group brings to the revision session a leaf on which the ink line of a drawing has been reworked in several places, with searching strokes and a visible correction near the shoulder of a figure. Another member observes that a handful of the drawings carry a thin green or brown wash, while the majority carry none. The group is preparing to describe how the drawings were made.

questions.stem: Your group sees reworked, searching ink lines and corrections in the Utrecht Psalter drawings, with only a few carrying any wash. Which description of the making fits best?

options.text: A first sketch later worked up, in which the drawings were meant to be painted over
options.misconception: treats finished drawings as a stage before painting

options.text: A botched commission, in which the corrections show the artist struggled and had to be corrected
options.misconception: reads a correction as evidence of a failure to execute

options.text: A copy from an older model, in which the searching line is the sign of tracing
options.misconception: reads a searching line as evidence of a tracing

options.text: A drawn thought process, in which the corrections and the searching line are left visible in the finished work

questions.explanation: The searching line and the corrections are left visible in finished work, so the drawings record thinking rather than accident or copying. A botched commission, a tracing and an unfinished sketch each misdescribe the leaf.
questions.hint: Ask what a correction that was kept in the drawing tells you.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The agitated line of the Ebbo Gospels evangelist portrait
questions.learningObjective: Set out the conditions for describing a manner as characteristic of a school
questions.stem: Comparing the Ebbo Gospels portrait with other miniatures in the same book, the group asks which two steps it needs before the difference is described as characteristic of a school. Which two steps does the group need?

options.text: Show the portrait is the largest in the book, then treat its size as the sign of a school
options.misconception: treats the size of a miniature as evidence of a school

options.text: Show the difference recurs across a group of manuscripts, then show it is not one artist's habit alone
Show the ink is different, then treat the difference of ink as the defining feature
options.misconception: defines a school by the material used

options.text: Show the workshop was wealthy, then treat its wealth as the origin of the manner
options.misconception: explains a working manner by the wealth of the patrons

questions.explanation: A manner is characteristic of a school only when it recurs across a group of manuscripts and is shown not to belong to a single artist. Size, ink and the wealth of a patron do not establish a school.
questions.hint: Ask how many manuscripts share the feature, and how many artists.
